I'm checking whether Cys4's sulfur atom coordinates with the iron-sulfur cluster in this protein, calculating the distance from its SG atom to Fe1 and finding it's too far (~4.37 Å) to be a direct ligand.

Actually, checking Cys38, Cys41, and Cys6 against Fe1/Fe2, I find bond-length distances (~2.3 Å) confirming those are the true cluster ligands, and Cys4's SG also comes in at ~2.34 Å to Fe2 — so Cys4 is indeed a cluster-coordinating cysteine, which typically means it's buried. I'm now trying to estimate its solvent burial by counting nearby atoms within a reasonable radius of its backbone and sidechain positions.

Checking a few more nearby residues - Val34 and Val3 side chains are within range but Thr32 is too far to count as a contact.

The SG sulfur seems partially buried since it's small and largely determined by CB/SG exposure. I'm considering whether this cluster, coordinated by four cysteines, sits near the protein surface or interior by checking the iron atom's position relative to the overall protein extent.

Now I'm working through nearby residues within a several-angstrom radius of the sulfur atom to estimate its solvent accessibility, checking distances to Val3, Leu5, and other neighboring backbone and sidechain atoms.

Continuing to check distances between nearby residues, now looking at Cys4 and Gln7 atoms relative to the reference point.

I'm now also computing distances for Val34's CB, CG1, CA, and C atoms to see if they fall within range.

Continuing outward, Gly35's N and CA are within a reasonable 3.7-4.6 Å shell, while Cys38's SG and Cys41's CA are farther out around 6 Å or more, so they're less likely part of the immediate coordination sphere. It looks like the sulfur is surrounded by a fairly complete shell of nearby atoms.

This is consistent with a rubredoxin/ferredoxin-like fold where Cys4 and Cys41 ligate one iron while Cys6 and Cys38 ligate the other—these cluster-binding cysteines are typically buried with relative SASA under 10-20%, even though the cluster site itself sits near the surface. Given the backbone atoms of Cys4 seem only partially exposed at most, I'll conclude the sulfur is buried.
